Fri close, flat after EPS miss and guidance cut

geo_headlines: STOCKS ROSE TO END THE WEEK. Friday the S&P 500 rose 0.59% to 7,811.54, 0.09% below Tuesday's record close. The Dow rose 0.83% and the Nasdaq 100 0.51%; chips slipped 0.41%. **For the week the S&P 500 gained 1.15%, the Dow 0.93% and the Nasdaq 100 0.24%, and the Nasdaq Composite had its fourth straight weekly gain (Investopedia).** VIX 14.84.

SPACEX HIT THE PHONE COMPANIES. SpaceX agreed to buy a nationwide low-band spectrum portfolio for Starlink Mobile, pending FCC approval. T-Mobile, AT&T and Verizon fell 8.5% to 13%, the S&P 500's three worst performers, while tower owners Crown Castle, SBA and American Tower rose 7% to 16% (Investopedia).

OIL ROSE AS ISAIAS SHUT GULF OUTPUT. Brent December settled at $104.72 (+0.42%) and WTI November at $91.85 (+0.39%), recovering from early losses after Trump's Iran pledge as producers halted more than 70% of US Gulf crude output (Reuters via Nation Thailand). Gold $4,216.30 (+1.4%).

ISAIAS MADE LANDFALL NEAR DESTIN. The storm came ashore Friday night on the Florida Panhandle as a Category 2 hurricane with 105 mph winds and was no longer a hurricane by early Saturday (AP). Hundreds of thousands lost power (New York Times).

IRAN: TALKS AND THREATS. At a Friday rally Trump said the Iran war would end quickly "one way or the other" (Al Jazeera). The Kremlin said Trump welcomed Russia's help toward a settlement, and Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it struck an LPG carrier south of the Strait of Hormuz (Al Jazeera).

SENTIMENT FELL; DELTA CUT ITS OUTLOOK. Michigan sentiment fell to 46.3 from 48.1 (47.6 expected); current conditions hit a record low of 44.7, and year-ahead inflation expectations rose to 4.7% (TheStreet). Delta earned $1.72 a share against $1.88 expected and cut its 2026 forecast on a 62% jump in fuel costs (24/7 Wall St., Yahoo Finance).

BONDS: 10-YEAR 5.24%. The 10-year rose 2bp Friday to 5.24% but fell 4bp on the week; the 2-year rose to 4.80%. FedWatch: October hike 18.8%, December 84.3%, from 84.8%. The cash bond market is closed Monday for Columbus Day; stocks are open.
client_frame_short: Stocks finished a good week near their highs. The S&P 500 rose 1.2% and closed Friday less than a tenth of a percent below Tuesday's record, even with oil above $100 and a hurricane hitting the Gulf Coast. **The two things to watch next week are inflation on Wednesday and the first big-bank earnings on Tuesday.** Consumers feel worse about current conditions than at any point in the survey's history, and that gap between how people feel and how markets are doing is a useful talking point. For clients, no changes are needed.
client_frame:
If a client calls this weekend, the story is a market that keeps climbing despite a lot of noise.

The week: the S&P 500 gained 1.15% and the Dow 0.93%. Thursday's AI scare, a report that OpenAI's revenue was about $20 billion below earlier figures, was mostly reversed by Friday.

The mood gap: Michigan consumer sentiment fell to 46.3, and the current-conditions gauge hit a record low. People are frustrated by prices: year-ahead inflation expectations rose to 4.7%. Yet stocks sit near their highs. That gap is normal. Sentiment surveys track how households feel about prices today, while stock prices track expected corporate earnings. Historically, very low sentiment readings have not been reliable sell signals; markets have often done well in the year after sentiment troughs, because the bad news is already in prices.

Oil and the storm: Hurricane Isaias hit the Florida Panhandle as a Category 2 and weakened by Saturday morning. More than 70% of Gulf oil output was shut ahead of it, which kept Brent at $104.72. Delta cut its forecast because its fuel bill rose 62%, a reminder that high oil acts like a tax on some businesses and consumers, even as energy producers benefit.

Iran: Trump said he won't strike before the November 3 midterms but also said the war would end "one way or the other." The risk has been pushed back, not removed.

Next week: inflation (CPI) on Wednesday at 8:30 AM, two weeks before the Fed's October 28 decision, and JPMorgan, Goldman, Citi and Wells Fargo report on Tuesday.

For clients, the message holds: high-quality bonds pay more than 5% for a decade, and long-term equity plans do not need changing. What would change the view: a 10-year close above 5.40% (now 5.24%), a 30-year above 5.75% (now 5.60%), or actual US strikes on Iran that keep Brent well above $105 (now $104.72).
